event.title: Bhopal 1984, the gas cleared, the poison did not
event.summary: On the night of 2-3 December 1984, methyl isocyanate leaked from the Union Carbide pesticide plant in Bhopal. Thousands were killed or injured within hours. Forty years on, Amnesty and Indian regulators still document toxic waste and groundwater contamination around the abandoned site.
event.hero: A night of gas. Four decades of poisoned water.

nodes.title: MIC gas flooded neighbourhoods overnight
nodes.description: On the night of 2-3 December 1984, methyl isocyanate leaked from the Union Carbide India Limited pesticide plant in Bhopal. The gas moved into nearby neighbourhoods. Amnesty International records this as one of the worst industrial catastrophes and corporate negligence cases in living memory. Thousands were killed or injured within hours.

nodes.title: Mass death and lifelong disability
nodes.description: The leak caused immediate deaths and left survivors with lifelong disability. Chronic illness among gas-exposed families is part of the first catastrophe, not a later footnote. That health burden still shapes the city forty years on.

nodes.title: The plant had already been poisoning soil and water
nodes.description: Before the night of the leak, the plant had already been releasing dangerous chemicals. Amnesty documents spillages, accidents, and dumping into air, soil, and groundwater during operations. That slower poisoning is what Amnesty calls the second catastrophe. It began while the factory was still running.

nodes.title: The site was left with toxic stockpiles
nodes.description: After operations ended, the site was left without adequate disposal. Amnesty finds thousands of tonnes of toxic waste remained buried in and around the plant. Those stockpiles kept feeding soil and water contamination long after the gas had cleared.

nodes.title: Groundwater contamination persists into the 2020s
nodes.description: Central Ground Water Authority sampling for the National Green Tribunal in 2023-24 took 72 groundwater samples within 5 km of the plant. Nitrate exceeded BIS limits at 7 sites. Iron exceeded limits at 11 sites. Manganese exceeded limits at 3 sites. Other WHO and BIS exceedances showed up for phosphate, sodium, potassium, and hardness. Most tested heavy metals were within limits.

nodes.title: Communities still face unsafe water risk
nodes.description: Contaminated wells sit in the same neighbourhoods that survived the gas. Unsafe water adds a second exposure pathway on top of the 1984 leak. Families living near the plant still face that combined risk.

nodes.title: Accountability and remediation lagged for decades
nodes.description: Amnesty’s 40-year review finds clean-up and justice still incomplete. Survivors have waited decades for full remediation. Accountability lagged while contamination continued.

nodes.title: 2024: regulators are still sampling the plume
nodes.description: The National Green Tribunal took suo motu notice after December 2023 reporting on toxic waste and water risk. That action forced a fresh CGWA investigation. The contamination is still being measured, not only remembered.

nodes.title: Full remediation cost remains open
nodes.description: Until permanent waste removal and water remediation finish, exposure pathways remain open. Clean-up and compensation tallies keep shifting as new contamination data appears. No single audited cost total is used here.

claims.text: Amnesty International (2024) records that the December 1984 methyl isocyanate leak in Bhopal was one of the worst industrial catastrophes and corporate negligence cases in living memory.
Amnesty finds that during plant operation, spillages, accidents, and dumping released dangerous chemicals into air, soil, and groundwater.
Amnesty finds that after the site was abandoned without adequate disposal, thousands of tonnes of toxic waste remained buried in and around the plant.

A Central Ground Water Authority investigation for the National Green Tribunal (OA 03/2024) took 72 groundwater samples within 5 km of the plant. Nitrate exceeded BIS limits at 7 sites. Iron exceeded limits at 11 sites. Manganese exceeded limits at 3 sites. Other WHO and BIS exceedances showed up for phosphate, sodium, potassium, and hardness. Most tested heavy metals were within limits.
Amnesty’s 40-year review finds that survivors still face incomplete remediation and justice gaps decades after the leak.
The National Green Tribunal took suo motu cognizance after December 2023 reporting on toxic waste and water risk. That action prompted the fresh CGWA study.
Researchers and regulators are still measuring the remaining cost. Until permanent waste removal and water remediation finish, exposure pathways remain open.
claims.caveat: No single audited cost total used here.

predictions.title: Contamination remains locally detectable 40 years on
predictions.method: Treat CGWA exceedance counts as the verified present-day bound.
predictions.caveat: Spatial pattern can change with monsoon and pumping.

sources.title: New govt study shows high groundwater contamination in some areas

timeline.label: Gas leak
timeline.detail: 2–3 Dec 1984, MIC release over Bhopal neighbourhoods.

timeline.label: Site abandoned with waste
timeline.detail: Toxic stockpiles remain. The groundwater pathway continues.

timeline.label: 40 years of injustice
timeline.detail: Amnesty 2024 + CGWA/NGT sampling still find contamination.

timeline.label: Remediation unfinished
timeline.detail: Clean-up and safe water remain open obligations.

what_we_know: The December 1984 methyl isocyanate leak killed and injured thousands in Bhopal.
Amnesty documents a second catastrophe of dumped waste and incomplete clean-up.
2023-24 CGWA sampling still found selected groundwater exceedances within 5 km of the plant.
what_remains_uncertain: How far the contamination plume extends, and how it has moved over time.
The full health and economic cost of second-generation exposure.
